nodes.location: Front of the upper arm, at the surface: its two heads start on the shoulder blade, join, and cross the elbow to the radius.
nodes.whatItDoes: Bends your elbow and turns your palm up; with the elbow bent it is the strongest palm-up muscle. It also crosses the shoulder, where references describe only weak help raising the arm forward.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute most of the front contour of the upper arm above the elbow crease, since it is the surface muscle there. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

These are group results from short studies, not a forecast for any one person, and they are not used to weight credit.

sources.title: Kholinne et al., The different role of each head of the triceps brachii muscle in elbow extension (Acta Orthopaedica et Traumatologica Turcica 52(3):201-205, 2018)

sources.title: Maeo, Wu, Huang, Sakurai, Kusagawa, Sugiyama, Kanehisa and Isaka, Triceps brachii hypertrophy is substantially greater after elbow extension training performed in the overhead versus neutral arm position (European Journal of Sport Science 23(7):1240-1250, 2023)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): 21 adults did cable elbow extensions with one arm overhead and the other in a neutral position, five sets of ten at seven tenths of the one-repetition maximum, twice a week for 12 weeks; MRI muscle volume. Second review, 19 Oct 2026: an independent search confirmed the design and the volume results (whole muscle about 19.9 against 13.9, long head 28.5 against 19.6, lateral and medial heads 14.6 against 10.5, each per hundred), lower loads in the overhead arm and similar strength gains. Second review, 19 Oct 2026: an independent search confirmed the journal, volume and pages, the thin wire electrodes in the long head, the long arm brace locking the elbow straight with the forearm neutral, fast and slow motions with and without a 5-pound weight, and the conclusion that any shoulder role would be passive or tied to elbow and forearm activity. sources.title: Chalmers, Cip, Trombley, Cole, Wimmer, Romeo and Verma, Glenohumeral Function of the Long Head of the Biceps Muscle: An Electromyographic Analysis (Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 2(2), 2014)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): 13 healthy volunteers, surface EMG of both biceps heads, deltoid, infraspinatus and brachioradialis during shoulder motion with and without elbow splinting and a 1-kg load; mean activity in both biceps heads was low; long-head activity rose significantly with flexion and abduction, short-head activity did not. Second review, 19 Oct 2026: an independent search confirmed the abstract and PubMed id; its Table 4, as summarised, showed that with the elbow and forearm splinted, adding the 1-kg load raised long-head activity significantly only at 45 degrees of abduction and 90 degrees of flexion. The authors' conclusion section was not seen.

sources.title: Diplock, Hing and Marks, The long head of biceps at the shoulder: a scoping review (BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 24:232, 2023)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (opening of the abstract): 214 articles in six themes; the biceps' role in glenohumeral elevation and stability in healthy shoulders is minimal, larger with rotator cuff failure or an absent tendon. Its exact wording on EMG was not seen; volume and article number not shown. Second review, 19 Oct 2026: an independent search gave volume 24, article 232, a search of six databases to December 2021, and the same conclusion (little contribution to elevation and stability in healthy shoulders, a larger role with rotator cuff failure).

sources.title: Accessory heads of the biceps brachii muscle: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Journal of Anatomy, 2022)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract, via a Czech research-output record): 78 articles, 10,603 upper limbs, random-effects meta-analysis; accessory heads in a minority of limbs, a single accessory head the commonest form; more often unilateral and in males, no significant side difference; falling prevalence over time; innervation and blood supply nearly identical to the main muscle and usually asymptomatic. Authors were not shown; the journal is inferred from the DOI prefix; the year from the record id. Population subgroup results were not seen. Second review, 19 Oct 2026: an independent search showed the pooled prevalence, about one limb in ten (9.6 in 100, confidence interval 8 to 11), a single accessory head being the commonest form (8.4 in 100). The claim still gives no rate, following the palmaris longus rule. Authors still not shown.

sources.title: Tubbs, Oakes and Salter, The subanconeus muscle (Folia Morphologica 65(1):22-25, 2006)
sources.notes: Added by the second review. Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract, on the journal's site): 18 cadaveric elbows; deep fibres of the medial head of triceps attached to the posterior elbow capsule in every specimen, most densely near the ulnar nerve groove; no specimen had a distinct muscle belly; tension on these fibres compressed the capsule rather than retracting it, and the authors concluded that they do not retract the capsule with extension as had been theorised. singleSourceFunctionClaims: None among the six new function claims (each rests on three to five references, after the second review's changes).

The two shipped function claims the page reuses are single-source: forearm:biceps.function (A50) and forearm:brachialis.function (A51), as 03-anatomy-evidence.md §2 says. Corroborating references were found this time (see each shipped claim's upperArmUse); they are frozen claims, so adding sources is the database lane's call.
Non-function claims resting on one source: upper_arm.biceps.variation.1 (one meta-analysis) and upper_arm.triceps_long.selectivity.1 (one ten-person study).

elsevier.biceps_brachii: independent searches disagreed on whether it lists a shoulder action; now cited for the origins only.

disagreementsAndWording: Biceps at the shoulder: Kenhub and Loyola call it a weak flexor, TeachMeAnatomy lists shoulder flexion, Elsevier lists no shoulder action; EMG studies disagree (Levy: no long-head activity with the elbow braced; Chalmers: low activity rising with flexion and abduction) and a scoping review calls its part in raising the arm minimal in healthy shoulders. The function claim says 'weak help' and that one reference lists none; the selectivity claim states the EMG disagreement; no node action.
Biceps and forearm position: Coratella 2023 found more biceps activity palm up while lifting; Kleiber 2015 (A4) found no change. The selectivity claim states both.

Long head steadying the shoulder: StatPearls and IMAIOS say with the arm by the side (adducted); Radiopaedia says in abduction. The claim says it helps hold the head of the bone in its socket and names no arm position.

Long head shoulder adduction: Kenhub and IMAIOS list it; Radiopaedia lists extension only. The claim attributes both to 'references' and only extension becomes a node action (adduction is not an upper-arm region action).
Coracobrachialis adduction: Elsevier lists adduction first; Loyola and TeachMeAnatomy call it weak. The claim says 'helps draw it toward the body'.
Coracobrachialis insertion: Elsevier gives the middle third of the humerus, Loyola the upper half of its inner border. The claim says 'about halfway down'.

Brachialis edges: the shipped forearm claim says it 'may show at its sides'; this review confirmed only the outer edge (Kenhub video). The new upper-arm claim and the neutral shape note say outer edge; the shipped claim is frozen and stays on the forearm page.

Training studies on arm position (Maeo 2023: more volume gain overhead in every head; Stasinaki 2018: no difference) are stated together in a draft selectivity claim; the draft reason is the §1.2 / §8 policy conflict, not the evidence.
Akima et al. 2021 (PLOS One, PMC8174684): isometric surface EMG of the three heads; the abstract seen said activity mostly did not differ, but it was cut off mid-result, so it is not cited.
Triceps heads by force level (one older review: medial and lateral active from onset, long head at higher forces) was seen only second-hand and is not cited.

Medial head at the surface (second review): Radiopaedia says largely deep; Kenhub's article says overlapped by the long and lateral heads and its video says it cannot be felt; Madsen says its muscle reaches further toward the elbow. DocCheck Flexikon, the only source saying its lower part shows, was removed as a user-edited wiki. The appearance claim now says what the remaining sources say; the outcrop is weakly supported.

Biceps at the shoulder, Elsevier (second review): independent searches disagreed on whether Elsevier's biceps entries list assisting shoulder flexion, so the function claim no longer says that a reference lists none. Radiopaedia's action summary, as one search showed it, gives the long head abduction and the short head adduction and flexion at the shoulder; not cited, since the page's own wording was cut off.

Medial head and the elbow capsule (second review): Loyola says the medial head retracts the capsule on extension, and Elsevier says some fibres attach to the capsule (sometimes called articularis cubiti); Tubbs, Oakes and Salter (2006) found that pulling on these fibres compressed the capsule and did not retract it. The function claim states both; the node says what they do is debated.

Distal biceps tendon (second review, not cited): Eames et al. (2007) found the lower tendon in two distinct parts, one continuing from each head, in 10 of 17 cadaver elbows, and suggested the heads may act partly independently; Cho et al. (2011) found a split tendon in 12 of 25. The biceps caveat no longer says the heads 'end in one tendon'. No source found shows the heads differing in action, so §1.2's single biceps node stands.

Triceps insertion (second review): StatPearls and Elsevier describe one common tendon; Madsen found the medial head's own tendon deep to the common one, confluent at the olecranon. The claims now say the heads 'end together on the point of the elbow'.

Akima et al. 2021 (PLOS One, PMC8174684), seen again in the second review: at 20 to 80 per hundred of maximum isometric force and three elbow angles, surface EMG did not differ between the three heads except between the medial and lateral heads at the lowest force at 60 degrees; the abstract was cut off before the higher-force results, so it is still not cited.

Villalba et al. 2024 (International Journal of Strength and Conditioning 4(1)), seen in the second review: in single-arm push-downs, long-head EMG was highest with a palm-up handle; no lateral-head result was shown. A candidate long-head selectivity claim for the anatomy lane, not added here.
section12Checks: Layers: biceps surface, brachialis deep with a front outcrop, long and lateral heads surface, medial head deep with a back outcrop: supported (medial outcrop with a disagreement, above). Coracobrachialis deep: supported in part (felt in the armpit). No deviation.

Lateral and medial heads share every action: supported (both cross only the elbow and extend it). The medial head's pull on the elbow capsule is not a region action. Kholinne's modelled force difference by arm height is acute and does not change the actions; mappings stay 'shared'.
The biceps stays one node: supported. Its heads differ only at the shoulder (Chalmers: long-head activity rose with flexion and abduction, short head did not), where its role is weak.
Brachioradialis as an external: supported by the rule (prime mover of elbow.flexion; curls load it).

Observation outside §1.2: the forearm's anconeus carries catalogMuscleKey 'triceps' (forearm nodes.ts), the upper arm's catalog key; region catalog keys are explicit (§1.1), so this may be harmless, but the registry lane should look.

Region actions (second review): shoulder.flexion's only declared performer is the coracobrachialis, which is adjacent and cannot be mapped; with the biceps' row left out, no mappable upper-arm member performs shoulder.flexion. That is a lane decision (list the biceps row as assist, or record a §1.2 deviation removing the action). shoulder.extension: long head, assist. The long head and coracobrachialis also adduct the arm, which is not an upper-arm region action.

Parent node actions (second review): the triceps is kind 'muscle', role 'group' (§1.2), and the shared test requires a prime node action on every non-adjacent node of kind 'muscle'. See nodeActionsLeftOut.
Medial head outcrop (second review): weakly supported once DocCheck Flexikon was removed; kept as §1.2 has it, flagged for full-text or human review.
policyQuestions: upper_arm.triceps_long.selectivity.2 is draft because §1.2 sends long-head regional-growth findings to selectivity claims while §8 says selectivity claims are never growth. The owner or the adversarial review decides.
Second review: the biceps' shoulder-flexion row (assist) or a §1.2 deviation removing shoulder.flexion from the upper arm (nodeActionsLeftOut).
Second review: a prime elbow.extension row on the triceps parent, or a platform change exempting role 'group' from the 'every muscle a main action' test (nodeActionsLeftOut).
